items.tts: Picture plucking a guitar string. It bounces back and forth, making a steady sound that fades out slowly.
items.html: Picture plucking a guitar string. It bounces back and forth, making a steady sound.

items.tts: When you pull the string to the side, it naturally wants to snap back to its quiet resting spot.
items.html: When you pull the string to the side, it naturally wants to snap back to its quiet resting spot.

items.tts: That resting spot is called equilibrium. The pull that yanks the string back is the restoring force.
items.html: That resting spot is called equilibrium. The pull that yanks the string back is the restoring force.

items.tts: How far you pull the string from equilibrium is its amplitude. It is just the maximum stretch.
items.html: How far you pull the string from equilibrium is its amplitude. It is just the maximum stretch.

items.tts: The time for one bounce is the period, and frequency is bounces per second. They are exact opposites.
items.html: The time for one bounce is the period, and frequency is bounces per second: T = 1/f.

items.tts: For a weight on a spring, a heavier mass slows the bounce, but a stiffer spring speeds it up.
items.html: For a weight on a spring, a heavier mass slows the bounce, but a stiffer spring speeds it up: T = 2π√(m/k).

items.tts: Because the bounce makes a repeating wave, we can track the object's exact position using cosine.
items.html: Because the bounce makes a repeating wave, we can track the object's exact position: x(t) = A cos(ωt).
